newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - How to do business at any cost.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - How to do business at any cost.

text.p: It's six in the morning and the plane wheels hit the tarmac. It's the start of a busy week in a foreign city for an international business executive.
But how much company money is he or she likely to spend during the impending business trip? That, of course, depends upon the city of arrival.
A Reuters straw poll of business costs around the world, conducted in more than 30 cities during February, illustrates how vast the differences can be.

First, to the airport car hire counter, where a week's rental, without discounts, of a mid-sized car can cost anything from just over $200 in Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, to around $1,000 in Rio de Janeiro or Vienna.
Car types in the "mid-sized" band offered by international car hire firms vary hugely, but of course favourite sellers on the domestic market are likely to prevail.

A Ford Taurus would be a likely candidate for the rental car park at Dulles Airport in Washington, while a somewhat more modest Fiat Bravo would be more typical in Milan or Rome. At Narita outside Tokyo, for anyone brave enough to take on that city's traffic, a Nissan Sunny would be a probable option.
So the hire car comes cheaply in hyperinflationary Bulgaria, and our executive is about to find that most things are astonishing bargains, as long as you have a hard currency to offer.
HOTEL ROOMS AN EXCEPTION
The exception is hotel rooms, and on arrival in central Sofia the cost per night without discount is likely to be around $300.
Moscow is infamous for sky-high hotel prices and a non-discounted room there suitable for a foreign business executive can cost up to $400.
At the other end of the scale, France boasts a reputation for modest accommodation prices and a business-style hotel in central Paris may come as cheaply as $80. The Gallic ambience comes free.

A secretary or adminstrative assistant may be necessary for the deal in progress. Assuming some language skills are necessary, this can cost up to $50 an hour in Istanbul, as little as $5 in Moscow, or it may quite simply not exist at all.

In Russia, however, an armed bodyguard may be more of a requirement than a translator -- many Western business executives working in the former Soviet republics now have permanent shadows, armed and dangerous.

Want to drop out to a nearby cafe for a coffee? Near Times Square in New York you may find the latest flavoured cappuccino at $1.50, but it will cost you three times that if you want the same dose of caffeine with a view of Hong Kong harbour.
Back in Sofia, it may cost no more than a few cents, but flavoured cappuccino is hardly a likely prospect.

After a hard day's business, a spot of dinner is in line, and here cultural differences will dictate whether you pick at a plate of noodles off Japan's Ginza, or tuck into the best a French chef can offer in a Montmartre restaurant.

Aspiring to Western cuisine in a culture unused to it may have an expensive price tag -- a good three-course Italian meal for two with a bottle of Chianti in central Tokyo could cost $170, more than twice the likely cost of the same in Rome or Milan.
In Moscow, a Western-style meal would go for a staggering $175, while a similar dinner with a Bulgarian contact in Sofia, although perhaps not of the same standard, could cost as little as $6.
THE POLITICAL COST OF DOING BUSINESS
The cost of doing business is not simply an accounting exercise for the economy-minded business executive, in some places it is a political hot potato.
In Singapore last year, the cost of living was a fierce topic of debate in the election and the Department of Statistics produced an interesting snippet that eggs had not changed price for 50 years.

The same cannot be said for a Western style three-course meal for two with a bottle of wine -- the price tag could be $120, although some of the plentiful ethnic culinary experiences available in the city state would come in a lot cheaper.

If business for our executive goes badly there may be a requirement to seek solace in a bottle, and for comparison purposes Johnny Walker Red Label whisky has been used as the Reuters international benchmark.

The problems of doing business in Bulgaria can be obliterated at the cost of only $4.70 for the bottle, while in Singapore, our executive can expect to pay $56. In London, not far from the Scottish hills of its provenance, a bottle would cost around $18.

A night off at the cinema? A Hollywood blockbuster in Tokyo will cost around $15, whereas the same film, with different subtitles, will cost only a few cents in Bulgaria or around $10 in a multiplex cinema near the White House.
And if, drooping with exhaustion at the end of the trip, our executive just wants to get back to the airport and take off, he or she may have to think again.

It's just a 10-minute trip down the road to the departure terminals in Dubai or Zurich, Frankfurt is well-connected by road or rail, but it is a different matter in car-choked Tokyo, where the trip to Narita airport even by fast train takes nearly an hour. Moscow and Istanbul are difficult and snarl-ups on the way to New York's John F Kennedy can cause major problems.
